title: Memory types at a glance
summary: SRAM, DRAM, register files, ROM, eFuse, flash and the new non-volatile memories each store a bit in a different way. This topic compares them and shows how a ROM is described in SystemVerilog — and why `initial` blocks behave differently in simulation, FPGAs and ASICs.
objectives: Explain how SRAM, DRAM, ROM, flash, eFuse and MRAM store a bit.
Compare memory types by volatility, speed, density and endurance.
Write a ROM in SystemVerilog with case and with $readmemh.
Choose a suitable memory type for a given use.

subsections.title: How each memory stores a bit

blocks.md: Memories differ in **how a bit is physically stored**. That single fact decides speed, density, whether the data survives power-off, and how often it can be written. Click the cells:

blocks.caption: Storage principle of six memory types

spots.title: SRAM
spots.md: Two cross-coupled inverters hold the bit as long as power is on; two access transistors (A) connect it to the bit lines. **Fast**, no refresh, but 6 transistors per bit.

spots.title: DRAM
spots.md: The bit is **charge on a tiny capacitor**, reached through one transistor. Very dense, but the charge leaks: every row must be **refreshed** about every 64 ms, and reading destroys the charge (it is written back).

spots.title: Mask ROM
spots.md: At each crossing of word line and bit line a transistor is **present or absent** — decided when the chip is made. Cannot be changed.

spots.title: Flash
spots.md: Electrons trapped on an isolated **floating gate** shift the transistor's threshold voltage. Keeps data for years without power; writing and erasing are slow and wear the oxide out.

spots.title: eFuse / OTP
spots.md: A small link is **blown once** by a high current (eFuse) or an oxide is broken down (antifuse). Used for chip IDs, trimming and repair data.

spots.title: MRAM
spots.md: A magnetic tunnel junction: the **resistance** is low when the free layer is parallel to the fixed one, high when anti-parallel. Non-volatile, fast, nearly unlimited writes.

tabs.label: SRAM
tabs.md: Static RAM — the workhorse on chip: caches, buffers, scratch-pads, FPGA block RAM. Fast (sub-ns to few ns), needs no refresh, loses data at power-off. Generated by **memory compilers** for every size.

tabs.label: Register file
tabs.md: Small, very fast, **many ports** (e.g. 2 reads + 1 write per clock). Built from flip-flops or special multi-port cells.

tabs.label: DRAM
tabs.md: Dynamic RAM — 1T1C cells, very dense, separate chips (DDR, LPDDR) or stacked (HBM). Needs refresh; accessed by rows (*open a row, read columns*).

tabs.label: ROM
tabs.md: Content fixed at manufacturing: boot code, tables, microcode. Either a ROM macro or — for small tables — plain logic.

tabs.label: OTP / eFuse
tabs.md: Programmed **once** after manufacturing: serial numbers, calibration (trim) values, memory-repair information, security keys.

tabs.label: Flash
tabs.md: NOR flash (fast random reads, code storage) and NAND flash (dense, page-based, SSDs and memory cards). Erase before write; limited endurance.

tabs.label: Emerging
tabs.md: **MRAM** (magnetic), **ReRAM** (resistive filament), **PCM** (phase change). Non-volatile and faster than flash; used as embedded NVM in newer processes.

blocks.title: Questions to ask
blocks.md: How big? How fast? Must the data survive power-off? How often is it written? Can it be on the same chip (process support)? The answers usually leave only one or two candidates.

blocks.title: `initial` is not the same everywhere
blocks.md: In **simulation** `$readmemh` always works. In an **FPGA** the content becomes part of the bitstream — block RAM really starts with it. In an **ASIC**, an SRAM macro powers up with random content: an `initial` block on a RAM is ignored by synthesis. A ROM in an ASIC is made by a **ROM compiler** from the code file, or as logic for small tables.
